  "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — follow FIXED iteration schedules despite operating in a non-stationary learning landscape. STaR (NeurIPS 2022) generates rationales, filters for correctness, and fine-tunes for a predetermined number of iterations. ReST-EM (Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes this as Expectation-Maximization but observes diminishing returns after exactly 2-3 iterations without understanding WHY or WHEN to stop. Self-play methods (Absolute Zero, arXiv 2505.03335; R-Zero, arXiv 2508.05004) use fixed iteration structures despite the model's learning needs changing across iterations.

This fixed scheduling is suboptimal for three compounding reasons:

(1) CHANGING MODEL NEEDS: Early in self-improvement, the model benefits from broad data generation across difficulty levels. As training progresses, the model masters easy problems and needs targeted data at its capability frontier — the 'boundary-level' problems that HS-STaR (EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2505.19866) shows offer maximal learning utility. DART-Math (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2407.13690) demonstrates that standard generation has severe bias toward easy queries, wasting compute on problems the model has already mastered. But the frontier shifts during training, so static difficulty targeting is itself insufficient.

(2) UNPREDICTABLE SATURATION AND COLLAPSE: 'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444) shows that prolonged self-training leads to reward hacking and sudden complete performance collapse — but the onset is unpredictable and varies by model and dataset. ReST-EM's diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations may be premature stopping (the model could benefit from more cycles with targeted data) or too late (collapse has already begun). The model collapse literature (Shumailov et al., Nature 2024) establishes that iterative training on self-generated data degrades distribution tails, with 'Strong Model Collapse' (ICLR 2025) showing this persists even with mixed real/synthetic data.

(3) MISALIGNED GENERATION↔TRAINING BALANCE: RLVR (GRPO) improves pass@1 (sampling efficiency) but has limited capacity to expand the pass@k reasoning frontier beyond the base model (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up). This means RL phases eventually saturate and new synthetic data is needed to expand the frontier before RL can consolidate further. Conversely, generating too much data without sufficient RL consolidation wastes compute — the model needs to absorb existing knowledge before benefiting from new examples. The optimal balance between generation and training changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance.

Critically, the DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS to address these limitations already exist but have never been combined into a self-improvement scheduling framework: pass@k predicts RL outcomes with R² up to 0.88 (Quagmires, arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop); pass@k serves as an active training signal at per-step granularity (Pass@k Training, arXiv 2508.10751); entropy trajectory signals collapse (Entrocraft, arXiv 2604.26326; EntroPIC, arXiv 2511.15248); the generation-verification gap determines self-improvement potential and scales monotonically with pre-training compute (Mind the Gap, arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025); the solver-verifier gap predicts self-improvement trajectories as exponential curves toward a computable limit (arXiv 2507.00075). These diagnostic signals, developed for RLVR optimization and distillation, are even MORE valuable for self-improvement scheduling because self-improvement has higher collapse risk, self-generated data quality varies more than teacher-generated data, and the optimal generation↔training balance changes as the model improves.",
  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first diagnostic-guided adaptive scheduling framework for self-improvement cycles in mathematical reasoning. FrontierLoop uses frontier diagnostics — pass@k spectrum, entropy trajectory, difficulty-stratified performance — to make real-time phase-level decisions: WHEN to generate new synthetic data, WHAT difficulty to target, WHEN to switch to RL training, and WHEN to stop.

Four specific limitations of existing methods create this opportunity:

(a) FIXED ITERATION COUNTS: STaR and ReST-EM use predetermined iteration counts (typically 2-3). Mind the Gap (ICLR 2025) shows that self-improvement potential is governed by the generation-verification gap, which varies by model, task, and training stage — a fixed count cannot adapt to this. The solver-verifier gap theory (arXiv 2507.00075) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a limit, but the curve's parameters change across iterations as the model's distribution shifts.

(b) NO COLLAPSE DETECTION: Self-training can lead to reward hacking and complete collapse (arXiv 2505.21444), but no self-improvement method monitors for collapse in real time. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103) identifies 'Diversity Illusion' — where training signals appear diverse but collapse into recurring patterns — but addresses this within self-play, not through scheduled diagnostics.

(c) UNIFORM DATA GENERATION: Existing methods generate data uniformly across difficulty levels (STaR) or with static difficulty heuristics (DART-Math). Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, arXiv 2505.14970) uses MAB for adaptive category selection within a single RL run, but does not make the higher-level decision of whether to generate data AT ALL vs. train on existing data.

(d) NO GENERATION↔TRAINING SCHEDULING: SvS (Beyond Pass@1, arXiv 2508.14029) performs variational problem synthesis continuously during RLVR — at every step regardless of whether new data is needed. SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176) cycles rollout length within RL but doesn't alternate between data generation and training modes. Neither uses diagnostics to determine WHEN generation is productive vs. wasteful.

FrontierLoop's value proposition is COMPUTE EFFICIENCY: by generating data only when diagnostics indicate frontier stagnation, and targeting generation at the specific difficulty bands where the model is stuck, FrontierLoop avoids wasting compute on redundant data generation while preventing premature stopping. The theoretical grounding comes from three validated principles: (i) pass@k captures the model's latent capability that RL can consolidate (Quagmires); (ii) entropy trajectory predicts training stability (Entrocraft); (iii) the generation-verification gap determines the ceiling of self-improvement (Mind the Gap), providing a principled stopping criterion.",
  "landscape": "FOUNDATIONAL SELF-IMPROVEMENT METHODS:

STaR (arXiv 2203.14465, NeurIPS 2022, Zelikman et al.) is the foundational iterative self-improvement method: generate chain-of-thought rationales, filter for correctness, fine-tune, repeat. Includes 'rationalization' — providing the correct answer as a hint for failed problems. Demonstrated improvements on GSM8K and CommonsenseQA. FrontierLoop extends STaR's generate→filter→train loop with diagnostic-guided scheduling and RL-based training.

ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization: generate samples (E-step), filter by correctness (M-step), iterate. On MATH and APPS with PaLM-2, model-generated data yielded larger gains than human-written data. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop addresses this by using diagnostics to determine whether diminishing returns signal genuine saturation or suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on BOTH correct and incorrect solutions from the STaR loop. 7B V-STaR surpasses LLaMA2 70B on GSM8K. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier as an enhanced filtering mechanism during generation phases.

SELF-PLAY AND ZERO-DATA METHODS:

Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335, 2025) achieves SOTA on coding and math reasoning with ZERO external data via self-play: a single model proposes tasks and solves them, with code execution as the sole verifiable reward. R-Zero (arXiv 2508.05004, 2025) uses a Challenger-Solver co-evolutionary framework, achieving +6.49 points on math benchmarks with Qwen3-4B-Base over 3 iterations. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) identifies 'Diversity Illusion' in self-play and proposes Memory-Augmented Penalty and Skill-Aware Measurement. 'Towards Understanding Self-play for LLM Reasoning' (arXiv 2510.27072, NeurIPS 2025) finds self-play capacity is bounded by the base model and the proposer is the critical component.

FrontierLoop differs from self-play methods in two ways: (1) we use adaptive diagnostic-guided scheduling rather than fixed iteration structures; (2) our framework is agnostic to the data generation mechanism — it can use self-play (Absolute Zero-style), solution sampling (STaR-style), or problem synthesis (MathSmith-style) during generation phases, with the diagnostic module determining which is most productive.

ITERATIVE CYCLING METHODS — CLOSEST PRIOR WORK:

SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176, Wen et al., 2025) is the closest existing iterative cycling method for math reasoning. SIRI performs 3 iterations of compression↔expansion cycling during RL, oscillating rollout length between 8,192 and 16,384 tokens via a cosine scheduler. On AIME24, SIRI-low achieves 40.4% accuracy (vs. 28.2% baseline) with 46.9% token reduction. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION: SIRI cycles WITHIN RL (varying rollout length to control reasoning conciseness), while FrontierLoop cycles BETWEEN modes (data generation vs. RL training). SIRI does not generate new training data — it varies the RL training configuration. FrontierLoop could incorporate SIRI's compression↔expansion within its RL phases while adding the higher-level generation↔training scheduling.

ReMiT (arXiv 2602.03075, Feb 2026) performs iterative mid-training ↔ RL cycling, showing cascading improvements across two cycles (ReMiT → ReMiT2). While ReMiT operates at the pre-training ↔ post-training boundary, it validates that iterative cycling can compound.

Beyond Pass@1 / SvS (arXiv 2508.14029, Liang et al., 2025) synthesizes variational problems from correct solutions during RLVR, achieving +18.3% and +22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/AIME25. SvS performs continuous problem synthesis at every training step. FrontierLoop's key difference: diagnostic-gated generation — synthesize new data only when frontier diagnostics indicate stagnation, saving compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS AND SIGNALS:

Quagmires in SFT-RL Post-Training (arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop) trained hundreds of models up to 12B and found pass@64/pass@256 predict RL outcomes with R² up to 0.88 (2× over SFT score prediction). Used as a STATIC pre-RL predictor; FrontierLoop extends to DYNAMIC real-time monitoring during training.

Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751, ByteDance/RUC) uses pass@k directly as a per-step reward to balance exploration and exploitation, achieving 17.9% vs. 12.9% Pass@1 on Enigmata for Qwen2.5-7B. This validates pass@k as an active signal at per-step granularity; FrontierLoop uses it at phase-level diagnostic granularity for mode switching — complementary applications at different scales.

Entrocraft (arXiv 2604.26326, 2026) achieves ~17% improvement in pass@32 over GRPO through entropy-guided rejection sampling against a target entropy schedule. EntroPIC (arXiv 2511.15248, 2025) uses PID control to maintain target entropy during RLVR. Both validate entropy trajectory as a training stability diagnostic. FrontierLoop incorporates entropy monitoring as a collapse detection signal, using deviations from the expected entropy schedule to trigger mode switching.

Cover@tau (Beyond Pass@k, arXiv 2510.08325, 2025) measures the fraction of solvable problems where at least tau proportion of completions are correct, capturing genuine reasoning reliability vs. lucky sampling. More informative than raw pass@k for FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified diagnostics.

SELF-IMPROVEMENT THEORY:

Mind the Gap (arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025) formalizes self-improvement through the 'generation-verification gap' — when models verify better than they generate, self-improvement is possible. This gap scales monotonically with pre-training compute. Provides FrontierLoop's theoretical stopping criterion: when diagnostics indicate the generation-verification gap has narrowed to zero for a difficulty band, further self-improvement on that band is impossible.

Solver-Verifier Gap Theory (arXiv 2507.00075, 2025) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a limit determined by the solver-verifier gap. Validated across multiple models and datasets. Key finding: external data can be introduced at any stage without significantly affecting final performance — supporting FrontierLoop's flexible scheduling.

'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444, Shafayat et al., 2025) demonstrates both the promise and peril: self-training improves reasoning and feedback quality, but prolonged training causes reward hacking and complete collapse. FrontierLoop's collapse detection module directly addresses this.

Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Beyond the Base Model? (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up) shows RLVR improves pass@1 but does NOT expand pass@k frontier. This is FrontierLoop's central motivation: when RL reaches its pass@k ceiling, diagnostic-triggered data generation is needed to expand the frontier.

DIFFICULTY-AWARE AND EFFICIENT METHODS:

DART-Math (arXiv 2407.13690, NeurIPS 2024) identifies severe easy-query bias in standard generation and proposes Difficulty-Aware Rejection Sampling (DARS). HS-STaR (arXiv 2505.19866, EMNLP 2025) uses hierarchical pre-sampling with difficulty estimation to reallocate sampling budget toward 'boundary-level' problems. Self-Evolving Curriculum / SEC (arXiv 2505.14970, Chen, Bengio et al., 2025) formulates curriculum selection as a non-stationary MAB problem. MathSmith (arXiv 2508.05592, 2025) uses RL to optimize synthetic problem generation, jointly optimizing structural validity, reasoning complexity, and answer consistency.

FrontierLoop integrates insights from all four: DART-Math's difficulty awareness informs generation targeting; HS-STaR's boundary-level concept motivates frontier-difficulty generation; SEC's MAB formulation could enhance within-generation difficulty selection; MathSmith's RL-optimized generation is a candidate mechanism for FrontierLoop's generation phase.

HSIR / 'Better, Faster' (arXiv 2605.24998, May 2026) proposes verify-then-exit sampling and an Intrinsic Diversity score, achieving +10.9% performance with 42.4% less inference overhead. Orthogonal to FrontierLoop — HSIR improves efficiency WITHIN a self-improvement iteration; FrontierLoop optimizes scheduling ACROSS iterations. The two are composable.

RL on Incorrect Synthetic Data (arXiv 2406.14532, NeurIPS 2024) shows RL on incorrect traces is 8× more efficient than training on correct data alone. Motivates using both correct (for SFT/generation phase) and incorrect (for RL phase) self-generated data.

THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR MULTI-STAGE DESIGN:

'Large Language Model Post-Training: A Unified View' (arXiv 2604.07941, Zhao et al., Apr 2026) identifies three mechanisms structuring all post-training: support expansion, policy reshaping, and behavioral consolidation. FrontierLoop's two modes map directly: Generation Mode = support expansion (making new behaviors accessible), RL Mode = policy reshaping (improving within reachable regions). The paper's central thesis — 'progress increasingly depends on coordinated systems design' — provides theoretical justification for FrontierLoop's diagnostic-guided orchestration.

'Decoupling KL and Trajectories' (arXiv 2605.16826, May 2026) shows SFT, DAgger, offline RL, and OPD are points in a continuous design space defined by prefix source × KL direction. 'Post-Training is About States, Not Tokens' (arXiv 2605.22731, May 2026) argues state distribution — not loss function — is the primary differentiator of post-training methods. Both support FrontierLoop's approach: rather than claiming any single objective is optimal, we adaptively schedule modes that operate on different state distributions (model-generated for RL, frontier-targeted for generation).

CLPD (arXiv 2605.11260, May 2026) addresses teacher scheduling by progressively scheduling teachers of increasing capacity. PRISM (arXiv 2604.28123, Apr 2026) inserts distribution-alignment stages between SFT and RL. Both address multi-stage pipeline design but for supervised/distillation settings; FrontierLoop targets the pure self-improvement setting.

MATH-Beyond (arXiv 2510.11653, 2025) quantifies the RL/distillation frontier gap for mathematics. ProRL (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2505.24864) shows RL achieves substantial frontier expansion on logic puzzles (+54.8%) but limited expansion on math. 'Self-Improvement of Large Language Models: A Technical Overview' (arXiv 2603.25681, Mar 2026) surveys the field through the GRO (Generation-Reward-Optimization) framework. 'Limits of Generalization in RLVR' (arXiv 2510.27044, 2025) cautions that RLVR may reinforce superficial heuristics — motivating FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified diagnostics that can detect whether improvements are genuine.",

  "approach": "We propose FrontierLoop, the first diagnostic-guided adaptive scheduling framework for self-improvement cycles in mathematical reasoning. FrontierLoop operates in the PURE SELF-IMPROVEMENT REGIME: no external teacher model — the student generates its own synthetic data (reasoning traces and problems), with only a mathematical answer verifier as the external component (standard for RLVR). The core contribution is the SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK — a general mechanism for adaptively orchestrating when to generate new synthetic data, what difficulty to target, when to consolidate via RL, and when to stop — rather than any specific diagnostic metric.

ARCHITECTURAL OVERVIEW: FrontierLoop alternates between two modes, with transitions governed by a diagnostic module:

MODE 1 — GENERATION (Frontier Expansion / Support Expansion): Generate new synthetic training data targeted at the model's current capability frontier. Three generation mechanisms, selectable by the scheduler: (a) SOLUTION SAMPLING: for problems at the frontier difficulty, generate K solutions, filter for correctness (STaR-style), add to data pool; (b) VARIATIONAL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS: from existing correct solutions, synthesize structurally diverse problem variants with identical reference answers (SvS-inspired, arXiv 2508.14029); (c) RL-GUIDED PROBLEM GENERATION: use the model's own capabilities to generate new problems at target difficulty (MathSmith-inspired, arXiv 2508.05592). Difficulty targeting uses the Difficulty-Stratified Frontier Score (DSFS) to identify which difficulty bands have stalling pass@k.

MODE 2 — RL TRAINING (Consolidation / Policy Reshaping): Standard GRPO-based RLVR on the accumulated self-generated data pool. Entropy management via Entrocraft-style annealing schedule to prevent premature collapse. Both correct and incorrect self-generated traces are used: correct for positive rewards, incorrect for learning from errors (motivated by arXiv 2406.14532 showing RL on incorrect data is 8× more efficient).

DIAGNOSTIC MODULE: Evaluated on a compact held-out validation set (200 problems stratified by difficulty) every 100 training steps, computing:

(1) SAMPLING EFFICIENCY GAP (SEG) = pass@k − pass@1 (k=32): When SEG is large, the model has latent capability that RL can consolidate. When SEG is small AND pass@k is low, the model needs new data. Building on Quagmires' validation (pass@k predicts RL outcomes, R²=0.88) and Pass@k Training's validation (pass@k as active signal).

(2) DIFFICULTY-STRATIFIED FRONTIER SCORE (DSFS): Group validation problems into difficulty bands (easy/medium/hard/competition). Compute pass@32 for each band. Identify bands where pass@32 has stalled — these are where generation should target. Extends HS-STaR's 'boundary-level' concept from static pre-sampling to dynamic real-time targeting.

(3) ENTROPY TRAJECTORY: Policy entropy during RL training, compared against an expected annealing schedule. Entropy dropping below threshold despite regularization signals incipient collapse — trigger generation mode with temperature boost for diversity injection. Validated by Entrocraft and EntroPIC.

(4) SELF-CONSISTENCY DIVERGENCE (SCD): Gap between self-consistency accuracy (majority vote over K samples) and true accuracy (verified against ground truth). When self-consistency rises but true accuracy plateaus or drops, reward hacking is occurring (per arXiv 2505.21444). Trigger: pause training, evaluate, reduce RL intensity.

ADAPTIVE SCHEDULER — MODE SWITCHING LOGIC: Uses z-score-normalized thresholds (inspired by ZClip, arXiv 2504.02507) for cross-phase comparability:
- IF SEG is small (z < −1) AND pass@k_large stagnant (growth < ε per 500 steps) → Switch to GENERATION MODE (frontier exhausted, need new data)
- IF SEG is large (z > 0) AND entropy healthy (above schedule) → Stay in / switch to RL MODE (consolidate frontier into pass@1)
- IF entropy drops below 0.8× scheduled value → DIVERSITY INJECTION: generation with elevated temperature (1.2-1.5) targeting frontier difficulty
- IF SCD exceeds threshold (self-consistency diverging from ground truth) → EMERGENCY PAUSE: checkpoint, evaluate on held-out test, reduce RL learning rate
- IF pass@32 stagnant across ALL difficulty bands for 3 consecutive evaluations → STOP (generation-verification gap exhausted per Mind the Gap theory)

THEORETICAL GROUNDING: FrontierLoop's two modes map directly to the mechanisms identified in the Unified View of Post-Training (arXiv 2604.07941): Generation Mode performs SUPPORT EXPANSION (making new behaviors accessible by introducing training data at the frontier), while RL Mode performs POLICY RESHAPING (improving pass@1 within the currently reachable behavior space). The Unified View's thesis — 'progress increasingly depends on coordinated systems design' — motivates diagnostic-guided orchestration over fixed sequencing.

EXPERIMENTAL PLAN:

STAGE 0 — DIAGNOSTIC SIGNAL VALIDATION (1.5 weeks): Run a standard 3-iteration STaR loop on Qwen3-8B (or DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen3-8B), logging ALL four candidate diagnostics at every checkpoint. Analyze: (a) which signal best correlates with subsequent learning gain, (b) signal-to-noise ratio, (c) lead time (how early does each signal detect stagnation/collapse). Select the best diagnostic combination for subsequent stages.

STAGE 0.5 — CYCLING VALIDATION GATE (1.5 weeks): Single-cycle test: (i) RL training until diagnostic indicates frontier exhaustion → plateau pass@32 = P1; (ii) Difficulty-targeted generation → create new frontier data; (iii) Second RL phase → measure pass@32 = P2. GO/NO-GO: If P2 > P1 + 1pp on MATH-500, cycling validated → proceed to Stage 1. If P2 ≤ P1 + 1pp, cycling has no frontier expansion value → PIVOT to optimizing single-iteration diagnostic-guided self-improvement (still novel: when to stop generating, what difficulty to target, when to stop training). Either outcome produces a publishable contribution.

STAGE 1 — FULL EXPERIMENTS (4-5 weeks): If cycling validated: run FrontierLoop for up to 5 adaptive cycles, with the scheduler determining each phase's duration and the total number of cycles. If cycling invalidated: optimize single-iteration self-improvement with diagnostic-guided generation targeting and early stopping.

CORE BASELINES (6): (1) STaR with fixed 3 iterations — foundational comparison; (2) ReST-EM with fixed 2 iterations; (3) Pure RLVR (GRPO, no explicit generation phase); (4) Absolute Zero self-play (Zhao et al., 2025); (5) Fixed-interval cycling — generate every 2000 steps regardless of diagnostics (ablates the diagnostic guidance); (6) SvS-style continuous problem synthesis during RLVR.

KEY ABLATIONS (5): (1) Diagnostic signal comparison within FrontierLoop (SEG vs. entropy vs. DSFS vs. combined); (2) Adaptive vs. fixed scheduling (same total compute, different allocation); (3) Targeted vs. uniform difficulty in data generation; (4) With vs. without collapse prevention module; (5) Compute efficiency analysis: H100-hours per percentage point improvement.

EVALUATION: MATH-500, AIME 2024, LiveCodeBench. Report pass@1, pass@32, per-difficulty breakdowns, compute efficiency (H100-hours per point), number of adaptive cycles used, and collapse/divergence events. Additionally report Cover@tau (arXiv 2510.08325) for reasoning reliability.

COMPUTE ADVANTAGE: FrontierLoop operates entirely in the self-improvement regime — no expensive external teacher. All generation and training use the same 8B model. The diagnostic module adds ~15% compute overhead (pass@32 on 200 problems every 100 steps ≈ 15 min on 1×H100). The primary compute savings come from: (a) not generating redundant data when the current pool is sufficient (estimated 20-30% savings over fixed-schedule generation); (b) early stopping when diagnostics detect saturation or collapse (preventing wasted RL compute); (c) targeted generation at frontier difficulty (fewer samples needed per iteration than uniform generation, per DART-Math's findings).",

{
  "title": "FrontierLoop: Diagnostic-Guided Adaptive Self-Improvement Cycling for Mathematical Reasoning",
  "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — follow FIXED iteration schedules despite operating in a non-stationary learning landscape. STaR (NeurIPS 2022) generates rationales, filters for correctness, and fine-tunes for a predetermined number of iterations. ReST-EM (Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes this as Expectation-Maximization but observes diminishing returns after exactly 2-3 iterations without understanding WHY or WHEN to stop. Self-play methods (Absolute Zero, arXiv 2505.03335; R-Zero, arXiv 2508.05004) use fixed iteration structures despite the model's learning needs changing across iterations.

This fixed scheduling is suboptimal for three compounding reasons:

(1) CHANGING MODEL NEEDS: Early in self-improvement, the model benefits from broad data generation across difficulty levels. As training progresses, the model masters easy problems and needs targeted data at its capability frontier — the 'boundary-level' problems that HS-STaR (EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2505.19866) shows offer maximal learning utility. DART-Math (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2407.13690) demonstrates that standard generation has severe bias toward easy queries, wasting compute on problems the model has already mastered. But the frontier shifts during training, so static difficulty targeting is itself insufficient.

(2) UNPREDICTABLE SATURATION AND COLLAPSE: 'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444) shows that prolonged self-training leads to reward hacking and sudden complete performance collapse — but the onset is unpredictable and varies by model and dataset. ReST-EM's diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations may be premature stopping (the model could benefit from more cycles with targeted data) or too late (collapse has already begun). The model collapse literature (Shumailov et al., Nature 2024) establishes that iterative training on self-generated data degrades distribution tails, with 'Strong Model Collapse' (ICLR 2025) showing this persists even with mixed real/synthetic data.

(3) MISALIGNED GENERATION↔TRAINING BALANCE: RLVR (GRPO) improves pass@1 (sampling efficiency) but has limited capacity to expand the pass@k reasoning frontier beyond the base model (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up). This means RL phases eventually saturate and new synthetic data is needed to expand the frontier before RL can consolidate further. Conversely, generating too much data without sufficient RL consolidation wastes compute — the model needs to absorb existing knowledge before benefiting from new examples. The optimal balance between generation and training changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance.

Critically, the DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS to address these limitations already exist but have never been combined into a self-improvement scheduling framework: pass@k predicts RL outcomes with R² up to 0.88 (Quagmires, arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop); pass@k serves as an active training signal at per-step granularity (Pass@k Training, arXiv 2508.10751); entropy trajectory signals collapse (Entrocraft, arXiv 2604.26326; EntroPIC, arXiv 2511.15248); the generation-verification gap determines self-improvement potential and scales monotonically with pre-training compute (Mind the Gap, arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025); the solver-verifier gap predicts self-improvement trajectories as exponential curves toward a computable limit (arXiv 2507.00075). These diagnostic signals, developed for RLVR optimization and distillation, are even MORE valuable for self-improvement scheduling because self-improvement has higher collapse risk, self-generated data quality varies more than teacher-generated data, and the optimal generation↔training balance changes as the model improves.",
  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first diagnostic-guided adaptive scheduling framework for self-improvement cycles in mathematical reasoning. FrontierLoop uses frontier diagnostics — pass@k spectrum, entropy trajectory, difficulty-stratified performance — to make real-time phase-level decisions: WHEN to generate new synthetic data, WHAT difficulty to target, WHEN to switch to RL training, and WHEN to stop.

Four specific limitations of existing methods create this opportunity:

(a) FIXED ITERATION COUNTS: STaR and ReST-EM use predetermined iteration counts (typically 2-3). Mind the Gap (ICLR 2025) shows that self-improvement potential is governed by the generation-verification gap, which varies by model, task, and training stage — a fixed count cannot adapt to this. The solver-verifier gap theory (arXiv 2507.00075) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a limit, but the curve's parameters change across iterations as the model's distribution shifts.

(b) NO COLLAPSE DETECTION: Self-training can lead to reward hacking and complete collapse (arXiv 2505.21444), but no self-improvement method monitors for collapse in real time. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103) identifies 'Diversity Illusion' — where training signals appear diverse but collapse into recurring patterns — but addresses this within self-play, not through scheduled diagnostics.

(c) UNIFORM DATA GENERATION: Existing methods generate data uniformly across difficulty levels (STaR) or with static difficulty heuristics (DART-Math). Self-Evolving Curriculum (SEC, arXiv 2505.14970) uses MAB for adaptive category selection within a single RL run, but does not make the higher-level decision of whether to generate data AT ALL vs. train on existing data.

(d) NO GENERATION↔TRAINING SCHEDULING: SvS (Beyond Pass@1, arXiv 2508.14029) performs variational problem synthesis continuously during RLVR — at every step regardless of whether new data is needed. SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176) cycles rollout length within RL but doesn't alternate between data generation and training modes. Neither uses diagnostics to determine WHEN generation is productive vs. wasteful.

FrontierLoop's value proposition is COMPUTE EFFICIENCY: by generating data only when diagnostics indicate frontier stagnation, and targeting generation at the specific difficulty bands where the model is stuck, FrontierLoop avoids wasting compute on redundant data generation while preventing premature stopping. The theoretical grounding comes from three validated principles: (i) pass@k captures the model's latent capability that RL can consolidate (Quagmires); (ii) entropy trajectory predicts training stability (Entrocraft); (iii) the generation-verification gap determines the ceiling of self-improvement (Mind the Gap), providing a principled stopping criterion.",
  "landscape": "FOUNDATIONAL SELF-IMPROVEMENT METHODS:

STaR (arXiv 2203.14465, NeurIPS 2022, Zelikman et al.) is the foundational iterative self-improvement method: generate chain-of-thought rationales, filter for correctness, fine-tune, repeat. Includes 'rationalization' — providing the correct answer as a hint for failed problems. Demonstrated improvements on GSM8K and CommonsenseQA. FrontierLoop extends STaR's generate→filter→train loop with diagnostic-guided scheduling and RL-based training.

ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization: generate samples (E-step), filter by correctness (M-step), iterate. On MATH and APPS with PaLM-2, model-generated data yielded larger gains than human-written data. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop addresses this by using diagnostics to determine whether diminishing returns signal genuine saturation or suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on BOTH correct and incorrect solutions from the STaR loop. 7B V-STaR surpasses LLaMA2 70B on GSM8K. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier as an enhanced filtering mechanism during generation phases.

SELF-PLAY AND ZERO-DATA METHODS:

Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335, 2025) achieves SOTA on coding and math reasoning with ZERO external data via self-play: a single model proposes tasks and solves them, with code execution as the sole verifiable reward. R-Zero (arXiv 2508.05004, 2025) uses a Challenger-Solver co-evolutionary framework, achieving +6.49 points on math benchmarks with Qwen3-4B-Base over 3 iterations. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) identifies 'Diversity Illusion' in self-play and proposes Memory-Augmented Penalty and Skill-Aware Measurement. 'Towards Understanding Self-play for LLM Reasoning' (arXiv 2510.27072, NeurIPS 2025) finds self-play capacity is bounded by the base model and the proposer is the critical component.

FrontierLoop differs from self-play methods in two ways: (1) we use adaptive diagnostic-guided scheduling rather than fixed iteration structures; (2) our framework is agnostic to the data generation mechanism — it can use self-play (Absolute Zero-style), solution sampling (STaR-style), or problem synthesis (MathSmith-style) during generation phases, with the diagnostic module determining which is most productive.

ITERATIVE CYCLING METHODS — CLOSEST PRIOR WORK:

SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176, Wen et al., 2025) is the closest existing iterative cycling method for math reasoning. SIRI performs 3 iterations of compression↔expansion cycling during RL, oscillating rollout length between 8,192 and 16,384 tokens via a cosine scheduler. On AIME24, SIRI-low achieves 40.4% accuracy (vs. 28.2% baseline) with 46.9% token reduction. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION: SIRI cycles WITHIN RL (varying rollout length to control reasoning conciseness), while FrontierLoop cycles BETWEEN modes (data generation vs. RL training). SIRI does not generate new training data — it varies the RL training configuration. FrontierLoop could incorporate SIRI's compression↔expansion within its RL phases while adding the higher-level generation↔training scheduling.

ReMiT (arXiv 2602.03075, Feb 2026) performs iterative mid-training ↔ RL cycling, showing cascading improvements across two cycles (ReMiT → ReMiT2). While ReMiT operates at the pre-training ↔ post-training boundary, it validates that iterative cycling can compound.

Beyond Pass@1 / SvS (arXiv 2508.14029, Liang et al., 2025) synthesizes variational problems from correct solutions during RLVR, achieving +18.3% and +22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/AIME25. SvS performs continuous problem synthesis at every training step. FrontierLoop's key difference: diagnostic-gated generation — synthesize new data only when frontier diagnostics indicate stagnation, saving compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS AND SIGNALS:

Quagmires in SFT-RL Post-Training (arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop) trained hundreds of models up to 12B and found pass@64/pass@256 predict RL outcomes with R² up to 0.88 (2× over SFT score prediction). Used as a STATIC pre-RL predictor; FrontierLoop extends to DYNAMIC real-time monitoring during training.

Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751, ByteDance/RUC) uses pass@k directly as a per-step reward to balance exploration and exploitation, achieving 17.9% vs. 12.9% Pass@1 on Enigmata for Qwen2.5-7B. This validates pass@k as an active signal at per-step granularity; FrontierLoop uses it at phase-level diagnostic granularity for mode switching — complementary applications at different scales.

Entrocraft (arXiv 2604.26326, 2026) achieves ~17% improvement in pass@32 over GRPO through entropy-guided rejection sampling against a target entropy schedule. EntroPIC (arXiv 2511.15248, 2025) uses PID control to maintain target entropy during RLVR. Both validate entropy trajectory as a training stability diagnostic. FrontierLoop incorporates entropy monitoring as a collapse detection signal, using deviations from the expected entropy schedule to trigger mode switching.

Cover@tau (Beyond Pass@k, arXiv 2510.08325, 2025) measures the fraction of solvable problems where at least tau proportion of completions are correct, capturing genuine reasoning reliability vs. lucky sampling. More informative than raw pass@k for FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified diagnostics.

SELF-IMPROVEMENT THEORY:

Mind the Gap (arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025) formalizes self-improvement through the 'generation-verification gap' — when models verify better than they generate, self-improvement is possible. This gap scales monotonically with pre-training compute. Provides FrontierLoop's theoretical stopping criterion: when diagnostics indicate the generation-verification gap has narrowed to zero for a difficulty band, further self-improvement on that band is impossible.

Solver-Verifier Gap Theory (arXiv 2507.00075, 2025) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a limit determined by the solver-verifier gap. Validated across multiple models and datasets. Key finding: external data can be introduced at any stage without significantly affecting final performance — supporting FrontierLoop's flexible scheduling.

'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444, Shafayat et al., 2025) demonstrates both the promise and peril: self-training improves reasoning and feedback quality, but prolonged training causes reward hacking and complete collapse. FrontierLoop's collapse detection module directly addresses this.

Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Beyond the Base Model? (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up) shows RLVR improves pass@1 but does NOT expand pass@k frontier. This is FrontierLoop's central motivation: when RL reaches its pass@k ceiling, diagnostic-triggered data generation is needed to expand the frontier.

DIFFICULTY-AWARE AND EFFICIENT METHODS:

DART-Math (arXiv 2407.13690, NeurIPS 2024) identifies severe easy-query bias in standard generation and proposes Difficulty-Aware Rejection Sampling (DARS). HS-STaR (arXiv 2505.19866, EMNLP 2025) uses hierarchical pre-sampling with difficulty estimation to reallocate sampling budget toward 'boundary-level' problems. Self-Evolving Curriculum / SEC (arXiv 2505.14970, Chen, Bengio et al., 2025) formulates curriculum selection as a non-stationary MAB problem. MathSmith (arXiv 2508.05592, 2025) uses RL to optimize synthetic problem generation, jointly optimizing structural validity, reasoning complexity, and answer consistency.

FrontierLoop integrates insights from all four: DART-Math's difficulty awareness informs generation targeting; HS-STaR's boundary-level concept motivates frontier-difficulty generation; SEC's MAB formulation could enhance within-generation difficulty selection; MathSmith's RL-optimized generation is a candidate mechanism for FrontierLoop's generation phase.

HSIR / 'Better, Faster' (arXiv 2605.24998, May 2026) proposes verify-then-exit sampling and an Intrinsic Diversity score, achieving +10.9% performance with 42.4% less inference overhead. Orthogonal to FrontierLoop — HSIR improves efficiency WITHIN a self-improvement iteration; FrontierLoop optimizes scheduling ACROSS iterations. The two are composable.

RL on Incorrect Synthetic Data (arXiv 2406.14532, NeurIPS 2024) shows RL on incorrect traces is 8× more efficient than training on correct data alone. Motivates using both correct (for SFT/generation phase) and incorrect (for RL phase) self-generated data.

THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR MULTI-STAGE DESIGN:

'Large Language Model Post-Training: A Unified View' (arXiv 2604.07941, Zhao et al., Apr 2026) identifies three mechanisms structuring all post-training: support expansion, policy reshaping, and behavioral consolidation. FrontierLoop's two modes map directly: Generation Mode = support expansion (making new behaviors accessible), RL Mode = policy reshaping (improving within reachable regions). The paper's central thesis — 'progress increasingly depends on coordinated systems design' — provides theoretical justification for FrontierLoop's diagnostic-guided orchestration.

'Decoupling KL and Trajectories' (arXiv 2605.16826, May 2026) shows SFT, DAgger, offline RL, and OPD are points in a continuous design space defined by prefix source × KL direction. 'Post-Training is About States, Not Tokens' (arXiv 2605.22731, May 2026) argues state distribution — not loss function — is the primary differentiator of post-training methods. Both support FrontierLoop's approach: rather than claiming any single objective is optimal, we adaptively schedule modes that operate on different state distributions (model-generated for RL, frontier-targeted for generation).

CLPD (arXiv 2605.11260, May 2026) addresses teacher scheduling by progressively scheduling teachers of increasing capacity. PRISM (arXiv 2604.28123, Apr 2026) inserts distribution-alignment stages between SFT and RL. Both address multi-stage pipeline design but for supervised/distillation settings; FrontierLoop targets the pure self-improvement setting.

MATH-Beyond (arXiv 2510.11653, 2025) quantifies the RL/distillation frontier gap for mathematics. # AdaSTaR: Adaptive Data Sampling for Self-Taught Reasoners

## Core Contribution

AdaSTaR addresses inefficiencies in Self-Taught Reasoners (STaR) training by replacing random data sampling with adaptive mechanisms. The fundamental problem it solves is that "random observation (data) sampling" leads to "trained observation imbalance; inefficiently over-training on solved examples while under-training on challenging ones."

## Adaptive Mechanisms

The algorithm integrates two key adaptive sampling principles:

1. **Adaptive Sampling for Diversity**: Promotes balanced training across observations, preventing the model from repeatedly training on already-solved examples.

2. **Adaptive Sampling for Curriculum**: Dynamically adjusts data difficulty to match the model's evolving capabilities, implementing curriculum learning within the STaR framework.

## Performance Results

Across six benchmarks, AdaSTaR demonstrates:
- **Best test accuracy on all instances (6/6)**
- **58.6% average reduction in training FLOPs** compared to extensive baselines
- Improvements that "generalize to different pre-trained LMs and larger models"

## Publication Status

- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2025
- **arXiv ID**: 2505.16322
- **Submission Timeline**: Initial submission May 22, 2025; final revision October 6, 2025

The paper emphasizes that these efficiency and performance gains create "a pathway for more efficient and effective self-improving LMs."

# SePT: Self-Evolving Post-Training - Technical Details

## Core Mechanism

SePT operates through an iterative loop that "alternates between self-generation and training on self-generated responses." The cycling structure appears to be **adaptive rather than fixed**, with a critical mechanism called **online data refresh**.

## Generation-Training Cycle

The process works as follows:

1. **Self-Generation Phase**: The model samples questions and generates responses "under a specified sampling temperature"
2. **Training Phase**: The model trains itself on the newly generated data
3. **Online Data Refresh**: Each successive batch is "generated by the most recently updated model," ensuring the training data evolves as the model improves

This adaptive approach distinguishes SePT from static self-training, as the model continuously updates its own generation quality.

## Key Findings

**Benchmarks**: The method was evaluated across "six math reasoning benchmarks"

**Results**: SePT demonstrated improvements over "a strong no-training baseline, defined as the untuned base model evaluated at its best swept decoding temperature"

**Model Coverage**: Testing occurred "on several tested models"

## Core Contribution

The primary innovation is demonstrating that "language models improve their reasoning performance without external rewards, using only their own sampled responses for training." Ablations highlighted "the importance of online data refresh and temperature dynamics" in the approach's success.

# SOAR Framework: Technical Summary

Based on the arXiv paper abstract, here are the key technical details available:

## Bilevel Meta-RL Architecture
SOAR employs a two-model system: "A teacher copy of the model proposes synthetic problems for a student copy, and is rewarded with its improvement on a small subset of hard problems." This creates a meta-reinforcement learning loop where the teacher learns to generate pedagogically useful content.

## Measured Student Progress
The critical innovation is grounding the curriculum in observable learning outcomes rather than proxy metrics. The abstract emphasizes that "SOAR grounds the curriculum in measured student progress rather than intrinsic proxy rewards," distinguishing it from prior self-play approaches that suffered from instability.

## Key Findings
1. **Sparse reward learning**: The framework enables "bi-level meta-RL that unlocks learning under sparse, binary rewards" by leveraging latent model capacities
2. **Reward scheme superiority**: "Grounded rewards outperform intrinsic reward schemes used in prior LLM self-play, reliably avoiding the instability and diversity collapse modes"
3. **Quality over correctness**: Analysis reveals "structural quality and well-posedness are more critical for learning progress than solution correctness"

## Results
Testing on the hardest mathematical problem subsets (0/128 initial success rate) demonstrated the approach can escape reasoning plateaus without additional curated data.

A blog post with additional details is referenced but not provided in this content.

# SAI-DPO Technical Overview

## Core Mechanism

SAI-DPO (Self-Aware Iterative Data Persistent Optimization) operates as a dynamic sampling framework that recalibrates training data based on model evolution. The system uses two primary metrics:

**Knowledge Semantic Alignment**: Targets domain-specific weaknesses in the model's performance.

**Self-Aware Difficulty**: Derived from "pass rates and reasoning path characteristics, to gauge instance complexity relative to the model's current state."

## Adaptive Process

The framework employs iterative recalibration through "real-time feedback" mechanisms that dynamically adjust which training samples align with the model's changing competence level. Rather than static, externally-defined selection criteria, SAI-DPO continuously monitors the model's capability state and adjusts accordingly.

## Benchmark Results

The research evaluated performance across eight benchmarks, including AIME24 and AMC23 (competitive mathematics exams). Results show SAI-DPO "outperforms static baselines at most nearly 6 points" while achieving efficiency gains with "significantly less data."

## Publication Context

The work was submitted to ACL 2026 Findings, with revision history spanning May 2025 to April 2026, suggesting ongoing refinement of the approach.

# B-STaR Technical Mechanism Summary

## 1. **Parameters Adjusted**

B-STaR dynamically modifies:
- **Sampling temperature**: Ranges from 0.5 to 1.2 in 0.1 increments, controlling response diversity
- **Reward threshold (τ)**: Ranges from -1.0 to 1.0, determining selection strictness
- **Sample size**: Kept fixed at maximum budget (64 for math, 32 for coding)

The method "adjusts temperature and threshold automatically at every iteration" based on balance score optimization.

## 2. **Balance Score Metric**

Formula: `bs_i = min(n'_i/n⋆, 1) · (n'_i/n_i)`

Where:
- `n'_i` = unique correct responses per query
- `n_i` = total selected responses
- `n⋆` = target correct responses per query (computed as ⌈N/M⌉)

The metric captures both absolute quantity and quality ratio of selected responses, with a maximum value of 1.

## 3. **Exploration & Exploitation Monitoring**

**Exploration metrics**:
- Pass@K: At least one correct response among K samples
- Pass@K-S: At least S unique correct responses among K samples
- Distinct Equations: Proportion of unique equations in correct solutions

**Exploitation metrics**:
- Best-of-K accuracy: Whether top-ranked response is correct
- Reward@K-S: Whether top S candidates ranked by reward are all correct

## 4. **Training Framework**

B-STaR operates within the online RFT framework, not switching modes. It performs four iterative steps per cycle:
- Generate candidates at selected temperature
- Evaluate via fixed reward model
- Filter using dynamic threshold
- Fine-tune policy model via SFT loss

## 5. **Problem Generation**

The method only samples solutions from existing queries—"it does not generate new problems." It reuses the training dataset across iterations.

## 6. **Math Benchmark Results**

On Mistral-7B with online RFT:
- **GSM8K**: 53.8 Pass@1 (vs. 46.8 baseline)
- **MATH**: 27.8 Pass@1 (vs. 23.2 baseline)
- **MATH Pass@32**: 67.2 (vs. 62.6 baseline)

On Llama-3.1-8B:
- **GSM8K**: 61.6 Pass@1
- **MATH**: 29.2 Pass@1

## 7. **Iteration Count**

Experiments ran "9 iterations" with 500-step intervals (4,500 total steps). Configuration adjustments occurred at each iteration milestone.

# AdaSTaR: Detailed Mechanism Analysis

## 1) Solve-Rate Signals

AdaSTaR employs a "win statistic" (w_i) that captures the success rate of each observation. This is computed as "the proportion of correct answers out of K CoT samples generated at iteration t~i." The metric tracks model performance without requiring additional forward passes, reusing samples already inherent to the STaR pipeline.

## 2) Adaptive Sampling Algorithm

# Pass@k Training Mechanism: Core Technical Details

## 1) Advantage Function Definition

The advantage is **per-response**, not per-token. In standard GRPO, each token in a response shares the same advantage value. Pass@k Training maintains this structure but modifies how that advantage is computed.

## 2) Group-Level Advantage Computation

Yes, Pass@k Training operates at a **group level**. The mechanism works as follows:

- Rollout N responses
- Partition into groups of k responses each
- Assign a **group reward** based on whether "at least one response in the group is correct"
- Distribute this group advantage equally to all k responses within that group

## 3) Exact Mathematical Formulation

The group reward follows this logic:

> "the group reward is computed by the maximum among the rewards of the responses belonging to it"

Mathematically (from Eq. 5): Pass@k computes the "expected maximum reward obtained from the k sampled responses." A group receives positive reward if ANY member is correct.

The analytical advantage formulas are:

- **Positive responses**: `Â_pos = (1 - R̄^group) / σ^group`
- **Negative responses**: `Â_neg = (1 - R̄^group - (N_neg-1 choose k-1)/(N_rollout-1 choose k-1)) × (σ^group)^-1`

## 4) Key Differences from Standard GRPO

| Aspect | GRPO (Pass@1) | Pass@k |
|--------|---------------|---------|
| Reward Signal | Individual response correctness | Whether ≥1 correct in k-response group |
| Grouping | None | k responses form evaluation units |
| Focus | Exploiting confident solutions | Exploring diverse solution spaces |
| Entropy Preservation | Decreases over training | Naturally maintains higher entropy |

Standard GRPO rewards individual responses; Pass@k rewards group-level success.

## 5) Benchmark Results

Key reported achievements:

- **Qwen 2.5-7B on Enigmata**: Reaches **17.9 Pass@1** (vs. **12.9** for Pass@1 Training alone), surpassing **Claude-3.7-Sonnet (22.7)**
- **Out-of-Domain Transfer**: Qwen 2.5-7B achieves **7.1 Pass@1 on AIME 2025** (vs. 5.4 for Pass@1 Training)
- **32B Model**: Achieves **46.8 Pass@1** on Enigmata after combining Pass@k + Pass@1 training

The method enables "7B LLM to surpass the powerful LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o and Claude-3.7)" through sequential Pass@k then Pass@1 training.

### core_problem

Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — but operates entirely within SFT, cannot switch to RL, and cannot generate new problems beyond the fixed training set. ### approach

We propose FrontierLoop, the first framework using diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. Unlike prior within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR adjusts parameters within SFT; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling within STaR; SwS synthesizes problems within RL), FrontierLoop makes the higher-level decision of WHICH training regime is most productive at any given moment.

FrontierLoop operates in the PURE SELF-IMPROVEMENT REGIME: no external teacher — the student generates its own synthetic data with only a mathematical answer verifier as external component (standard for RLVR).

ARCHITECTURAL OVERVIEW: FrontierLoop alternates between two modes with qualitatively different compute profiles, governed by a diagnostic module:

MODE 1 — GENERATION (Frontier Expansion / Support Expansion): Generate new synthetic training data targeted at the model's current capability frontier. Three generation mechanisms, selectable by the scheduler: (a) SOLUTION SAMPLING: for problems at frontier difficulty, generate K solutions, filter for correctness (STaR-style); (b) VARIATIONAL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS: from correct solutions, synthesize structurally diverse problem variants (SvS-inspired); (c) WEAKNESS-TARGETED GENERATION: identify difficulty bands where pass@k stalls, generate new problems in those bands (extending SwS's within-RL weakness diagnosis to mode-level triggering). Within this mode, B-STaR-style temperature adaptation and AdaSTaR-style priority sampling can be applied — FrontierLoop's mode scheduling is orthogonal to and composable with within-mode adaptation.

MODE 2 — RL TRAINING (Consolidation / Policy Reshaping): GRPO-based RLVR on the accumulated data pool. Entropy management via Entrocraft-style annealing to prevent collapse. Both correct and incorrect traces used (motivated by arXiv 2406.14532: RL on incorrect data is 8× more efficient). Within this mode, SwS-style weakness detection and SEC-style category selection can operate — again orthogonal to mode scheduling.

DIAGNOSTIC MODULE: Evaluated on a compact held-out validation set (200 problems stratified by difficulty) every 100 training steps:

(1) SAMPLING EFFICIENCY GAP (SEG) = pass@k − pass@1 (k=32): When SEG is large, the model has latent capability that RL can consolidate → stay in RL. When SEG is small AND pass@k is low, the frontier is exhausted → switch to GENERATION. Building on Quagmires' validation (pass@64 predicts RL outcomes, R²=0.87 on Llama3-8B; combined predictor R²=0.94) and Pass@k Training's validation of pass@k as active group-level signal.

(2) DIFFICULTY-STRATIFIED FRONTIER SCORE (DSFS): Group validation problems into difficulty bands. Compute pass@32 per band. Identify bands where pass@32 stalls → target generation at those bands. Extends HS-STaR's boundary concept and AdaSTaR's solve-rate curriculum from static/within-iteration to dynamic cross-mode targeting.

(3) ENTROPY TRAJECTORY: Policy entropy during RL, compared against expected annealing schedule. Entropy dropping below threshold signals incipient collapse → trigger generation with elevated temperature for diversity injection. Validated by Entrocraft and EntroPIC.

(4) SELF-CONSISTENCY DIVERGENCE (SCD): Gap between self-consistency accuracy (majority vote over K samples) and verified accuracy. When self-consistency rises but true accuracy plateaus → reward hacking (per arXiv 2505.21444). Trigger: pause RL, evaluate, reduce learning rate.

- IF SEG small (z < -1) AND pass@k stagnant (growth < ε per 500 steps) → Switch to GENERATION (frontier exhausted)

### core_problem

Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) alternates generation and SFT in fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostic guidance. - WITHIN-PARADIGM ADAPTIVE METHODS (B-STaR, AdaSTaR): Adapt hyperparameters within STaR/SFT. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — but operates entirely within SFT, cannot switch to RL, and cannot generate new problems beyond the fixed training set. AdaSTaR (NeurIPS 2025) uses solve-rate signals for adaptive data sampling with 58.6% FLOPs reduction — but adjusts WHICH data to sample, not WHETHER to generate new data or train differently.

- WITHIN-RL ADAPTIVE METHODS (SwS, SEC, SIRI): Adapt within RL training. SwS (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.08989) identifies weaknesses during RL and synthesizes targeted problems — but performs synthesis continuously, not diagnostically triggered. SIRI cycles rollout length within RL. SEC uses MAB for category selection within RL.

- CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS (SvS): Synthesizes new problems at every RLVR step regardless of need, wasting compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

The key insight is that RL and data generation have COMPLEMENTARY failure modes: RL saturates when pass@k plateaus (it cannot expand the frontier beyond the base model's latent capabilities, arXiv 2504.13837), while data generation is wasteful when the model hasn't consolidated its existing knowledge (large Sampling Efficiency Gap means RL can still improve pass@1 without new data). The hierarchy of adaptive self-improvement decisions clarifies FrontierLoop's contribution:

Level 1 — TOKEN/GROUP-LEVEL: Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751) computes group-level advantages to balance exploration/exploitation within single RL steps.

Level 3 — PARAMETER-LEVEL: B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds across STaR iterations.
Level 4 — WITHIN-MODE: SwS synthesizes targeted problems within RL; SEC selects problem categories within RL; SIRI varies rollout length within RL.

(a) NO MODE SWITCHING: B-STaR (ICLR 2025) is the strongest existing diagnostic-adaptive method, but it operates entirely within online RFT (SFT). ### approach

We propose FrontierLoop, the first framework using diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. Unlike prior within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR adjusts parameters within SFT; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling within STaR; SwS synthesizes problems within RL), FrontierLoop makes the higher-level decision of WHICH training regime is most productive at any given moment.

FrontierLoop operates in the PURE SELF-IMPROVEMENT REGIME: no external teacher — the student generates its own synthetic data with only a mathematical answer verifier as external component (standard for RLVR).

ARCHITECTURAL OVERVIEW: FrontierLoop alternates between two modes with qualitatively different compute profiles, governed by a diagnostic module:

MODE 1 — GENERATION (Frontier Expansion / Support Expansion): Generate new synthetic training data targeted at the model's current capability frontier. Three generation mechanisms, selectable by the scheduler: (a) SOLUTION SAMPLING: for problems at frontier difficulty, generate K solutions, filter for correctness (STaR-style); (b) VARIATIONAL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS: from correct solutions, synthesize structurally diverse problem variants (SvS-inspired); (c) WEAKNESS-TARGETED GENERATION: identify difficulty bands where pass@k stalls, generate new problems in those bands (extending SwS's within-RL weakness diagnosis to mode-level triggering). Within this mode, B-STaR-style temperature adaptation and AdaSTaR-style priority sampling can be applied — FrontierLoop's mode scheduling is orthogonal to and composable with within-mode adaptation.

MODE 2 — RL TRAINING (Consolidation / Policy Reshaping): GRPO-based RLVR on the accumulated data pool. Entropy management via Entrocraft-style annealing to prevent collapse. Both correct and incorrect traces used (motivated by arXiv 2406.14532: RL on incorrect data is 8× more efficient). Within this mode, SwS-style weakness detection and SEC-style category selection can operate — again orthogonal to mode scheduling.

DIAGNOSTIC MODULE: Evaluated on a compact held-out validation set (200 problems stratified by difficulty) every 100 training steps:

(1) SAMPLING EFFICIENCY GAP (SEG) = pass@k − pass@1 (k=32): When SEG is large, the model has latent capability that RL can consolidate → stay in RL. When SEG is small AND pass@k is low, the frontier is exhausted → switch to GENERATION. Building on Quagmires' validation (pass@64 predicts RL outcomes, R²=0.87 on Llama3-8B; combined predictor R²=0.94) and Pass@k Training's validation of pass@k as active group-level signal.

(2) DIFFICULTY-STRATIFIED FRONTIER SCORE (DSFS): Group validation problems into difficulty bands. Compute pass@32 per band. Identify bands where pass@32 stalls → target generation at those bands. Extends HS-STaR's boundary concept and AdaSTaR's solve-rate curriculum from static/within-iteration to dynamic cross-mode targeting.

(3) ENTROPY TRAJECTORY: Policy entropy during RL, compared against expected annealing schedule. Entropy dropping below threshold signals incipient collapse → trigger generation with elevated temperature for diversity injection. Validated by Entrocraft and EntroPIC.

(4) SELF-CONSISTENCY DIVERGENCE (SCD): Gap between self-consistency accuracy (majority vote over K samples) and verified accuracy. When self-consistency rises but true accuracy plateaus → reward hacking (per arXiv 2505.21444). Trigger: pause RL, evaluate, reduce learning rate.

ADAPTIVE SCHEDULER — MODE SWITCHING LOGIC (z-score-normalized thresholds for cross-phase comparability):
- IF SEG small (z < -1) AND pass@k stagnant (growth < ε per 500 steps) → Switch to GENERATION (frontier exhausted)
- IF SEG large (z > 0) AND entropy healthy → Stay in / switch to RL (consolidate)
- IF entropy below 0.8× scheduled value → DIVERSITY INJECTION: generation with elevated temperature (1.2-1.5)
- IF SCD exceeds threshold → EMERGENCY PAUSE: checkpoint, evaluate, reduce learning rate
- IF pass@32 stagnant across ALL bands for 3 consecutive evaluations → STOP (generation-verification gap exhausted per Mind the Gap)

Within Generation Mode: use AdaSTaR-style priority sampling (Level 2) and B-STaR-style temperature adaptation (Level 3). Within RL Mode: use SwS-style weakness detection (Level 4), SEC-style category selection (Level 4), and Pass@k Training-style group rewards (Level 1). This composability is a feature, not a limitation — each level addresses a different optimization granularity.

STAGE 0 — DIAGNOSTIC SIGNAL VALIDATION (1.5 weeks): Run a standard 3-iteration STaR loop on Qwen3-8B, logging all four diagnostic signals at every checkpoint. Analyze: (a) which signal best correlates with subsequent learning gain, (b) signal-to-noise ratio, (c) lead time for detecting stagnation/collapse.

STAGE 0.5 — CYCLING VALIDATION GATE (1.5 weeks): Single-cycle test: (i) RL until diagnostic indicates frontier exhaustion → plateau pass@32 = P1; (ii) Difficulty-targeted generation → create new frontier data; (iii) Second RL phase → measure pass@32 = P2. GO/NO-GO: If P2 > P1 + 1pp on MATH-500, cycling validated → proceed. If P2 ≤ P1 + 1pp → PIVOT to single-iteration diagnostic-guided self-improvement (optimizing when to stop generating, what difficulty to target within a single cycle — still novel at the mode-scheduling level).

STAGE 1 — FULL EXPERIMENTS (4-5 weeks): FrontierLoop for up to 5 adaptive cycles, with the scheduler determining each phase's duration and total cycle count.

If FrontierLoop outperforms both, it demonstrates that (a) adaptive scheduling beats fixed scheduling (vs. SePT) and (b) mode-level adaptation is more powerful than within-paradigm adaptation alone (vs. B-STaR).

Primary savings from: (a) not generating redundant data when RL can still consolidate (20-30% savings over fixed cycling); (b) early stopping on saturation/collapse; (c) targeted generation at frontier difficulty.

  "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) alternates generation and SFT in fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostic guidance. ReST-EM observes diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations without understanding whether to generate more data or switch to RL.

- WITHIN-PARADIGM ADAPTIVE METHODS (B-STaR, AdaSTaR): Adapt hyperparameters within STaR/SFT. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — powerful levers WITHIN the SFT paradigm. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. AdaSTaR (NeurIPS 2025) uses solve-rate signals for adaptive data sampling with 58.6% FLOPs reduction — but adjusts WHICH data to sample, not WHETHER to generate new data or train differently.

- WITHIN-RL ADAPTIVE METHODS (SwS, SEC, SIRI): Adapt within RL training. SwS (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.08989) identifies weaknesses during RL and synthesizes targeted problems — but performs synthesis continuously, not diagnostically triggered. SIRI cycles rollout length within RL. SEC uses MAB for category selection within RL.

- CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS (SvS): Synthesizes new problems at every RLVR step regardless of need, wasting compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first framework that uses diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. This extends prior work on within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR's parameter adjustment, AdaSTaR's data selection) to the higher-level orchestration decision that determines the training regime itself.

The hierarchy of adaptive self-improvement decisions clarifies FrontierLoop's contribution:

Level 1 — TOKEN/GROUP-LEVEL: Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751) computes group-level advantages to balance exploration/exploitation within single RL steps.
Level 2 — DATA-LEVEL: AdaSTaR adjusts which training examples to sample within iterations; HS-STaR targets boundary-difficulty problems; SAI-DPO (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2505.16176) recalibrates instance selection using pass-rate difficulty.
Level 3 — PARAMETER-LEVEL: B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds across STaR iterations.
Level 4 — WITHIN-MODE: SwS synthesizes targeted problems within RL; SEC selects problem categories within RL; SIRI varies rollout length within RL.
Level 5 — MODE-LEVEL (FrontierLoop): Switches between fundamentally different computational regimes — inference-only data generation vs. gradient-based RL training — with different compute profiles, optimization objectives, and data requirements.

(a) NO MODE SWITCHING: B-STaR (ICLR 2025) is the strongest existing diagnostic-adaptive method, but it operates entirely within online RFT (SFT). It adjusts sampling temperature and reward threshold to balance exploration/exploitation — powerful levers within SFT. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. FrontierLoop adds the mode-switching capability that B-STaR lacks.

(b) FIXED-SCHEDULE CYCLING: SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) demonstrates that alternating between self-generation and training improves reasoning (Pass@1: 22.7→39.5 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B), but uses fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostics. Generation phases may occur when RL could still consolidate existing knowledge; training phases may continue past saturation. FrontierLoop replaces SePT's fixed schedule with diagnostic-triggered transitions.

(c) NO CROSS-MODE DIAGNOSTICS: SwS (NeurIPS 2025) diagnoses weaknesses WITHIN RL to guide problem synthesis, and B-STaR diagnoses exploration/exploitation WITHIN SFT to adjust parameters. But no method uses diagnostics to decide WHICH mode is currently most productive. ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop uses diagnostics to distinguish genuine saturation from suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on both correct and incorrect STaR solutions. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier for enhanced filtering during generation phases.

DIAGNOSTIC-ADAPTIVE SELF-IMPROVEMENT — CLOSEST PRIOR WORK:

It does not generate new problems, does not incorporate RL training, and cannot switch between training modes. Its adaptation is at Level 3 (parameter adjustment); FrontierLoop operates at Level 5 (mode switching). B-STaR's insights are complementary — FrontierLoop could use B-STaR-style parameter adaptation WITHIN each mode while adding higher-level mode scheduling.

AdaSTaR (arXiv 2505.16322, NeurIPS 2025, Koh et al.) addresses data imbalance in STaR through adaptive sampling: a hierarchical min-heap priority system orders observations by last-sampled iteration and win-rate, with a curriculum component using training accuracy α as strength proxy (quadratic f(α)=α² for automatic difficulty scheduling). DIFFERENTIATION: AdaSTaR adapts WHICH data to sample (Level 2), not WHETHER to generate new data or switch training paradigms (Level 5). FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified generation targeting extends AdaSTaR's adaptive sampling from within-iteration data selection to cross-mode generation decisions.

SAI-DPO (arXiv 2505.16176, ACL 2026 Findings) uses pass-rate-derived difficulty metrics and knowledge semantic alignment for iterative DPO training recalibration, achieving ~6 point improvements on AIME24. Operates within DPO training; FrontierLoop extends pass-rate-based adaptation to mode-level scheduling.

GENERATION↔TRAINING CYCLING METHODS:

SePT (arXiv 2510.18814, 'A Model Can Help Itself,' 2025) is the key ablation baseline. SePT alternates between self-generation (low-temperature sampling) and SFT training in FIXED 3-epoch cycles with online data refresh — each new batch from the most recently updated model. Temperature annealed 0.6→1.0. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B: Pass@1/8/32 of 39.5/57.7/67.9 (from 22.7/47.3/61.0 baseline). CRITICAL: SePT proves generation↔training cycling works but uses NO diagnostic guidance.
